full_judgment:
2. The relevant facts for disposal of this civil appeal, in short, are that Sam Miah, predecessor of respondent Nos. 1-10 instituted Title Suit No. 47 of 1980 in the Court of Munsif Sadar, Sylhet against the appellants and respondent Nos.11-33 for a declaration that the suit land described in schedule-II to the plaint belonged to the plaintiff in maliki right and the record of rights in respect of the suit land in the names of the predecessors of the defendants is wrong and incorrect and for recovery of khas possession of the suit land described in schedule-III to the plaint. The suit was renumbered as Title Suit No.28 of 1990 on transfer to the Court of Additional Assistant Judge, Circuit Court, Sylhet. During pendency of the suit, Saru Miah died and his heirs, the present plaintiffs were substituted. 

 3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the land described in schedule-I of the plaint originally belonged to Mufti Zainuddin and others of Dargah Mahalla, Sylhet in maliki right. Sheikh Selim, father of Saru Miah, original plaintiff, was tenant [chakran] a service under the said landlords. While he [Sheikh Selim] was residing in one of the homesteads of the landlords at Longar Dewri with his family, he took a second wife and went to reside with the 2nd wife at Rajor Goli surrendering the possession of the said homestead in favour of landlords where he had been residing as service tenant. Sam Miah then took settlement of the land described in schedule-I to the plaint from the landlords and while residing there, took his mother with him, gave shelter to his other two brothers named Kantu Miah, predecessor of defendant No.1 and Charu Miah alias Abdul Khalique, predecessor of defendant Nos. 16-24 and also one Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-16 and another person named Jan Khan. Thereafter, the landlords instituted Title Suit No.80 of 1951 in the 1st Court of Munsif Sadar, Sylhet for declaration of their title in the land of schedule-I of the plaint and recovery of khas possession against Sheikh Selim, Sara Miah and others who had been residing there and got a decree for declaration of title only. Against the said judgment and decree, Sam Miah filed Titie Appeal No.259 of 1953 before the District Judge, but subsequently, compromised the dispute and then by a registered kabala dated 22.09.1954 purchased the right, title and interest of the landlords in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint and continued owning and possessing the same by his right of purchase. While possessing the same, plaintiff Saru Miah transferred 1 (one) powa land in favour of his brother, Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique out of the land described in schedule-I by registered kabala and also transferred .005 decimal land out of the land described in schedule-I in favour of Tunu Miah, son of his other brother-Kantu. Miah by registered deed of gift dated 08.12.1979. During the field survey of the last survey and operation, settlement the lard described in schedule-1 was recorded in the names of the plaintiff and his brother according to their share, but recently by the first part of Baishakh, 1386 BS, the plaintiff came to know that the land in schedule-II had been wrongly recorded in the names of late Kantu Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.1-11 and late Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-14 beyond his knowledge. Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah were very close relatives of the plaintiff and they having no place to live in, sought for temporary shelter to the plaintiff and the plaintiff on compassionate ground allowed them to live in the land described in schedule-III on condition to move therefrom on arrangement of accommodation elsewhere. The plaintiff having learnt about the wrong record of rights of the land described in schedule-II in the names of Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah, demanded to defendant Nos.1-14 for correction of the record of rights and asked them to vacate the land described in schedule-III lastly by the last part of Baishakh, 1386 BS. Said Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah had no right, title and interest whatsoever in the suit land. The wrong record of rights of the Land described in schedule-II to the plaint in the names of Kantu Miah and Rashid Miah has cast cloud over the title of the plaintiff. Hence, the plaintiff instituted the suit. 

 5. Defendant Nos.1 and 11 contested the suit contending, inter alia, that the land described in schedule-I originally belonged to Mufti Zainuddin and others in maliki right and Sheikh Selim was the service tenant who used to reside in the scheduled land with his famkly and gave some portion of his land to Rashid Miah to reside therein. After sometime, Zaminders filed Title Suit No.80 of 1951 in the Court of Munsif, Sylhet for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession by evicting Sheikh Selim and others. Sheikh Selim and his son-Chant Miah only contested the suit. In the said suit, the maliki right of the Zaminders was declared, but the prayer for recovery of possession was disallowed. After abolition of the Zamindari system by the operation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, Sheikh Selim became a tenant under the Government in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint and the rent receiving interests of the plaintiff which he purchased from the Zaminders was extinguished by operation of law. The plaintiff acquired no right to the possession of the suit land by his alleged purchase and that the plaintiff used to reside in the land described in schedule-I to the plaint with his father, Sheikh Selim. Thereafter, while possessing the land described in schedule-I, Sheikh Selim died leaving behind two sons named Kantu Miah and plaintiff-Saru Miah, one daughter Malika Bibi and four grandsons and three grand-daughters by his predeceased son, Sheikh Chart Miah @ Abdul Khalique and thus, by inheritance, the plaintiff acquired 1/7th share, Kantu Miah predecessor of defendant Nos. 1 and 11 got 2/7th share, the heirs of Chan: got 2/7th and daughter Malika got 1/7th share in the land described in schedule-1. Rashid Miah, predecessor of defendant Nos.12-14, was residing in a portion of the land described in schedule-1 to the plaint with the permission of Sheikh Selim and during the settlement operation, his name was recorded on the basis of possession though he has no title over the suit land. The record of rights in respect of Rashid Miah is not correct, it should have been recorded in the name of Sheikh Selim, Rashid Miah being a licensee the specific portion of land described in schedule-I under Sheikh Selim. The plaintiff Mliah sold .07 acre of land to Charu Abdul Khalique out of his share in the land described in schedule-I, he has subsisting interest in only to the plaint. 

 13. Mr. Md. Motahar Hossain, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1-10, contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the High Court Division rightly found that the Courts below did not approach the case in proper perspective and both the Courts below were required to find that the plaintiffs had prayed for correction of the record of rights and eviction of some persons from the disputed land described in the said schedule who were claimed to be in permissive possession in the land described in schedule-III to the plaint and the Courts below ought to have decided the owner-ship of the plaintiffs in actual quantum of land. He further contends that the High Court Division, rightly held that the finding of the trial Court has no basis in fact or law since it is evident from the plaint and depositions that the plaintiffs did not pray for evicting anyone from the land described in schedule-II to the plaint an6 for recovery of khas possession. The plaintiffs rather sought for declaration of title along with correction of the record of rights regarding the land described in schedule-II to the plaint and recovery of khas possession of the land described in schedule-III to the plaint by evicting defendant No.1 therefrom. He further submits that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the Appellate Court below without discussing the evidence of PWs' and DWs' in light of their pleadings affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court below and allowed Cross Objection No.5 of 1992 and, therefore, non-consideration of the oral evidence of the parties in light of their respective cases vitiated the impugned judgment and decree passed by the Courts below. He further contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as both the Courts below misconstrued the pleadings of the parties and the evidence on record and their erroneous findings that the land described in schedule-II to the plaint is possessed by the defendants, and the plaintiffs cannot get the relief of recovery of khas possession without praying for recovery of khas possession of the entire Land described in schedule-II to the plaint are totally baseless and misconceived one and, moreover, the trial Court below also came to the erroneous conclusion that the suit is barred by limitation and that the suit is not duly stamped and, on a clear wrong approach to the cases of the parties, and their respective evidence led the Courts below to arrive at the erroneous conclusion with regard to the plaintiffs' possession over the suit land which has occasioned a serious miscarriage of justice. He further contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as defendant Nos.1 and 11 filed a joint written statement, defendant Nos.2(Ka)-(Ga) filed another joint written statement, and defendant Nos.12 and 13 also filed another joint written statement denying the case of the plain-tiffs but the said defendants did not adduce any evidence in support of their written statements and, furthermore, the Appellate Court below without elaborate consideration of entire evidence, both oral and documentary, held that the plaintiffs have not proved their title in the land described in schedule-II to the plaint, and allowed the cross objection, although the trial Court below came to a clear finding that the plaintiffs have their title over the suit land but no possession was maintained by the plaintiffs and, thus, the Courts below committed an error of law in not holding that the plaintiffs have proved their case. He further contends that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as PW-2 stated in his deposition that he knows the plaintiff, Sam Miah, and his heirs and he also knows the father of plaintiff, Sam Miah, namely, Sheikha Selim, and he also stated that he knows Sheikh Selim since his childhood, and Pw-3, Rupon Miah, as substituted plaintiff deposed on behalf of the plaintiffs, and he supported the plaintiffs' case, and Pw-4 corroborated the plaintiffs' case. He further contends that Pws'- 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 8 corroborated the case of the plaint, but both the trial Court below and the Appellate Court below without considering the evidence of all the Pws' and Dws' dismissed the suit and, thus, non-consideration of the said evidence by the Courts below caused a serious miscarriage of justice. It is further submitted that they High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the trial Court below did not at all discuss the evidence of Pwsf-3, 4, 5, 7 ant 8 regarding the title and possession of the suit land, and the Appellate Court below also did not consider the same. It is further submitted that the High Court Division was justified in making the Rule absolute inasmuch as the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in Habibullah (Md)-Vs-Sher Ali Khan and others [57 DLR (AD) (2005) 55] held that the High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment and decree of the Courts below when the same has been made either upon misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence causing failure of justice. The High Court Division is also competent to set aside the judgment and decree of the Courts below when the same has been passed on the basis of evidence, which cannot be considered as legal evidence, and had the same been not taken into consideration, the judgment and decree would not have been one as has been made. It is further contended that the High Court Division rightly found that the Appellate Court below ought to have written the impugned judgment and decree upon the independent analysis of fact and law in a comprehensive manner and, as such, there was total non-consideration of evidence by the Appellate Court below as evident from the impugned judgment and decree and, therefore, it is required that the Appellate Court below in passing the fresh judgment and decree on remand shall consider the amendments made in the plaint and find the real substance of the plaint as it contains numerous amendments and, further, consider all relevant evidence and, accordingly, the suit was rightly sent on remand to the Appellate Court below to write out a fresh judgment and decree in light of observations mate by the High Court Division. 

 17. It appears from the judgment and decree of the trial Court that exhibit-1 was the saf-kabala deed whereby Saru Miah, predecessor of the present plaintiffs, owned the suit property described in schedule-I to the plaint because, by that time, there has been an acquisition of rent receiving interests under the ,East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and the Zaminders remained only as superior rent receiving owner and Sam Miah purchased that entitlement from Mufti Zainuddin [exhibit-1] and at the same time, he had the occupancy right under the Government. It is admitted that the plaintiff sold a quantum of land of .71/2 acre to his younger brother, Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique. It appears from exhibit sKaly that Sheikh Selim did not continue to stay in the house situated in the scheduled property in Longer Dewari rather after getting married for The second time, he started living with his wife in Rajar Goli, Sylhet and therefore, Sheikh Selim did not earn any right of occupancy under the landlord and so his name could not be recorded in the settlement operation. The trial Court after consideration of the evidence on record came to the conclusion that the plaintiff had occupancy right in the property described in schedule-I to the plaint and predecessor of defendant Nos.1-11/12/13 did not have title to the property described in schedule-II to the plaint by occupancy right and the defendants were in possession of the property described in schedule-II to the plaint and without a prayer for recovery of khas possession the suit is not maintainable. The trial Court also held that the suit was barred by limitation and the valuation of the suit property was not proper. The Appellate Court below without applying judicial mind concurred with the findings of the trial Court regarding dismissal of the suit and disposed of the appeal in the same tune of the trial Court. 

 19. It reveals from the evidence on record that Pw-2 knows plaintiff-Saru Miah and his heirs and he also knows Sheikh Selim, the father of plaintiff-Saru Miah from his boyhood. It appears that, there is no allegation from defendant Nos.1-11 regarding the incorrect record of rights in the name of Saru Miah in 15 decimals of land described in schedule-I and defendant Nos.l-11 did not give any description of non-appearance of the name of Maleka Bibi in the record of rights. They only claimed that Sheikh Selim was the tenant in the 1st scheduled land and he permitted Rashid Miah to reside on 7 decimals of land described in the same schedule and after his death, his heirs had been in possession. It is admitted fact that the Zaminders filed Title Suit No.80 of 1951 in the Court of Munsif, 1st Court, Sylhet against Sheikh Selim for khas possession and eviction of them. The Zaminders obtained a decree in the aforesaid suit, but no order was passed regarding eviction and Sheikh Selim and Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique contested the suit. It appears that according to exhibit-Ka (1), Sheikh Selim left the suit land and went to Razargoli. It further appears that according to exhibit-1, Saru Miah on 22.09.1954 by a registered deed purchased the scheduled land. He sold one powa land to Charu Miah @ Abdul Khalique and 0½ decimal of land to Tunu, son of Kantu Miah.
